name: TV DIABLO Windows
note: v3333: MEASURED against his live console: 2 of 422 sessions carry no t0 at all. n=30 is s_1789330829280_66296 with 753 frames and a reel dated 13 Sep 23:20, and n=50 is s_1788879402448_41906 with 10 frames dated 08 Sep 17:56. Both hold real footage and both sit in the river, but all four card sites derived the clock straight from t0 with a null fallback, so those two got no clock: the date rendered as an em-dash and the title fell back to Session N. He reported it as cards that never paint, and his shelf question about sessions spaced days apart is the same thing seen from the front. THE FALLBACK IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN A GUESS: a session id carries its own epoch ms in the form s underscore ms underscore n, and on all 12 sessions checked where both exist the embedded ms and t0 agree to the minute. mtime CANNOT serve and the law pins that it never appears in the helper: all 19 reels on disk carry an mtime from a single bulk pass on 16 Sep, skews of 1.8 to 53.1 days, so it reports two months of footage as simultaneous. Four hand-rolled copies of the clock became ONE definition. The law is a REACHABILITY check and not a presence one, so it fails if any site re-inlines the old expression, and the baseline case pins that t0 still wins when it exists because a fallback that overrides a real reading is worse than none. THE HEART ROW IS THE OTHER HALF: reel clocks asks whether every reel on disk can still yield an epoch from its id, because if reels are ever named differently the fallback stops working SILENTLY, with no test changing and no error raised. It reads ok on his tree with all 19 reels parseable, and returns UNKNOWN rather than clean where there is no hist directory. Three other date conversions are deliberately excluded and named in the helper comment: a day-set builder and a today-filter feed COUNTS, and widening a clock that feeds a count changes the count. 2 red-proofs PROVEN, 468 gates.
